O.outcome_detail: what practitioners most immediately need or want

cells.quote: Research strategies and products are not necessarily what practitioners most immediately need nor want
cells.note: The presentation states this as a reason to explore supportive roles beyond research, but provides no empirical comparison or outcome data.

O.outcome_detail: perceived benefits of the research partnership

cells.quote: In contrast to traditional notions of distant relationships between schools and “ivory tower” researchers, Uncapher and Santa Clara staff say they have benefitted immensely from their work together. The key: a collaborative, ongoing relationship built on trust, reciprocity, and mutual respect.
cells.note: Case-study participants' accounts; no formal comparison or effect size was reported.

D.treatment: RPP workshops with concrete equity-integration mechanisms
D.comparison: instructor practice and plans before the workshops

O.outcome_detail: instructor equity-minded classroom practices and planned practices

cells.quote: Timely RPP workshops featuring concrete mechanisms for integrating equity practices (e.g., Equitizing the Syllabus and Soliciting Early Student Feedback) influenced instructor practice in the fall term as well as their plans for spring 2022.
cells.note: The study text reports influence/change but does not specify a directional comparison, statistical test, or effect size; the comparison is inferred from the reported change in practice and plans.

D.treatment: RPDP representation of small and rural districts on review panels

O.outcome_detail: representation and participation of small and rural districts in statewide review panels

cells.quote: Through their work with the R15CC, NDE was able to overcome this challenge by leveraging the expertise of regional coordinators from the Northeast, Northwest, and Southern Regional Professional Development Programs (RPDPs) to adopt instructional materials in multiple content areas each year. This collaborative approach allowed small and rural districts, that may lack subject matter experts, to be represented by their respective RPDP.
cells.note: Descriptive program account; the study reports no quantitative outcome data or measured comparison.

O.outcome_detail: model-estimated learning rate for negative reward prediction errors

cells.quote: Post-hoc t-tests revealed that adolescents had a significantly increased learning rate for negative RPEs in chosen objects (αc−: adults: .49 ± .05, adolescents: .69 ± .05, t(34) = − 2.816, p = .04, multiple comparison corrected, Fig. 2)
cells.note: Natural age-group comparison; no random assignment.

O.outcome_detail: anterior insula response to negative reward prediction errors

cells.quote: Post-hoc t-tests of the three bins revealed that the interaction was caused by a significantly increased response to negative RPEs in adolescents compared to adults (t(34) = − 4.08, p < .001, corrected for multiple comparisons, Fig. 3C).
cells.note: Natural age-group comparison; no random assignment.

O.outcome_detail: positive RPE-related neural activation in putamen, vmPFC, amygdala and posterior cingulate

cells.quote: In our main effect analysis of RPEs in cognitive flexibility, we found areas which are typically positively correlated with RPEs (increasing RPEs elicit more activity) such as the putamen, ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC), amygdala and the posterior cingulate (Table 2).
cells.note: Whole-group random-effects fMRI analysis across all 36 participants; model-derived RPEs were entered as parametric modulators.

O.outcome_detail: negative RPE-related neural activation in anterior insula, dmPFC and dlPFC

cells.quote: The bilateral anterior insula (aIns), bilateral dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC), and the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex were significantly anticorrelated with RPEs (decreasing RPEs elicit more activity, Table 2, Fig. 3A).
cells.note: Whole-group random-effects fMRI analysis across all 36 participants; model-derived RPEs were entered as parametric modulators.
